messages.subject: Variable g(0) values at stratum level
messages.subject_clean: Variable g(0) values at stratum level
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
This question is about multipliers. I'm beginning an analysis of line transect survey data for arboreal nests in a coniferous forest setting. I used several dozen randomized sample points, each one containing 4 independent 100m line transects. The age of the forest in these locations covers a span of more than 200 years. It is a foregone conclusion that g(0)<1 in most of the sample areas. I designed the study with the means to estimate g(0) in each location, but it's a safe assumption that g(0) will decrease as forest age increases. This means that I will have unique g(0) values for each of my strata categories. I've come across the following passage in the Distance user's guide:

In this version of Distance you can only define Multipliers in the global data layer. This means that you cannot account for factors that vary by stratum or transect. In future versions of Distance we hope to offer the ability to define multipliers at any level of the data hierarchy.

Has anyone invented a way around this limitation? I think that stratified g(0) values are a fact of this study.
Thanks!
Chad

messages.subject: Number of detections increases further from 0
messages.subject_clean: Number of detections increases further from 0
messages.body_plain:
I created distance intervals and placed observations in bins during the survey (we were not permitted to get exact distances in the field). I have a centerline and 3 bins of increasing width. I made a distance histogram for each of my ten surveys and almost all of them have the fewest detections in the 0 bin and the number of detections increases the further you get away from the centerline (see attached pdf). I have looked at other topics in the forum and in the Intro DS book and have noticed that evasive movements can cause fewer detections closer to the centerline. However, I believe the issue is that the animals were not uniformly distributed and the survey lines were not randomly placed with respect to that distribution.

I know that binning in the field is not recommended and 5-7 bins is much better than only 4. Also, I know that lines should be randomly placed with respect to animal distribution. However, I am wondering what issues might arise with fitting a detection function or deriving a density estimate from a dataset with these issues.

Thanks,

Bradley

messages.body_plain:
Meredith, when you do a run with multiple species, you're assuming that individuals of all species are equally detectable.  For common species, you should analyse one species at a time.  For rarer species, you could analyse them with more common species that you expect to have similar detectability, but you should not pool data across species with very different detectabilities - unless you ask Distance to fit a different detection function within each stratum (species).

A better option is probably to use the mcds engine of Distance, and specify species as a factor-type covariate.  This fits a common model across species, but allowing the scale of the detection function to vary by species.  You might still want to split your species into groups, so that species with very different detectabilities are not analysed together.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (CREEM) is hosting two linked workshops in the summer of 2015 in our purpose-built facilities at the University of St. Andrews, Scotland. The aim of these workshops is to train participants in the latest methods for design and analysis of distance sampling surveys, including line and point transects. The workshops are taught by leading researchers in the field, using industry-standard software.

The first workshop (11-14 August) will run at an introductory level, and will focus on distance sampling methods, largely described in the standard reference book "Introduction to Distance Sampling." The workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and participants will learn how to use the program "Distance." Participants will gain a solid grounding in both survey design and methods of analysis for distance sampling surveys.  Note that we have moved the 'automated survey design' and 'incorporating covariates in detection function' from the advanced workshop into the introductory workshop.

The advanced distance sampling workshop (17-20 August) will include advanced treatment of:  analyses in which detectability on the transect line is not assumed to be perfect (the so-called g(0) problem) and spatial (or  density surface) modelling. We will showcase a series of new R packages we have developed for performing standard as well as sophisticated analyses in R. The aim of this workshop is to bring participants up to date with the latest developments in distance sampling methods and software. It is also an opportunity for those actively engaged in the design, analysis and execution of distance sampling surveys to discuss common issues and problems, and set future research directions. The workshop will be a combination of lectures and computer sessions, with considerable time for discussion.

For all workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data sets, and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their data.  Computer sessions take place in our modern computer classroom (attached to the seminar room); participants can use our computers or bring their own laptops.

Additional details regarding the workshop can be found at our website

messages.subject: Reducing ferrying distance in survey design
messages.subject_clean: Reducing ferrying distance in survey design
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am designing a cetacean ship survey using DISTANCE. One fo my strata is coastal and is irregularly shaped, having deep concavities on both the coastal and seaward sides. As a result, the equal-spaced zigzag design has significant ferrying distances between the "points" of the zigzags, sometimes over 20 nm. This is a significant issue for a slow-moving ship, and reducing the non-productive ferrying time would be desirable.

I tried following the lead of Thomas et al. (2007) by dividing the stratum into 3 substrata to reduce the concavities. That does reduce the distances between the points, but because the starting points of the zigzags are random for each substratum, it does (sometimes) result in long ferry's going from the final transect in one substratum to the first transect in the next.

Having thought this over, it seems like the following procedure might produce an efficient design:

1. Divide the stratum into substrata appropriately to minimize concavities;
2. Set up designs for the substrata using the same effort intensity (i.e. effort allocated proportional to surface area);
3. Randomly select a survey for the first (i.e. in this case northernmost, since the survey axis runs N-S) substratum;
4. Deliberately select surveys for the remaining substrata to minimize ferrying between neigbouring substrata. Alternatively, generate the designs of the neigbouring substrata manually, using the endpoint of the previous substratum as the starting point of the next.

I know that it is normally not acceptable to deliberately select a survey from a design for operational reasons. However in this case the initial starting point (of the first substratum) would be selected randomly, so it follows that its endpoint should provide a random starting point for the next.

Does this procedure sound acceptable, or can anyone suggest something better?

Thanks,

Daniel Pike.

Each segment in a DSM analysis is given the location of its midpoint
(centroid). The "Effort" column accounts for this issue in the
modelling, as it defines the length of the segment -- so this is not a
problem during model fitting.

This will however look a little goofy if you plot the segments, as you
say the segments will be short. For plotting it's worth having an extra
set of columns in your data (e.g. "x_start", "x_end", "y_start",
"y_end") that you can use when you want the correct segment locations to
be plotted.

I hope this helps!

best,
--dave

messages.body_plain: My question is about right truncation of detection functions. I know Buckland et al. 2001 recommend truncating at g(x)=0.10, which is what I am doing. However, many papers that use Distance sampling compare AIC values for different model types (half-normal, hazard rate etc.) to pick the best model, but they apply the same truncation distance to each of the models. What I'm wondering is, if setting the truncation distance to the distance where g(x)=0.10 depends on the detection function itself, shouldn't there be a different truncation distance for each model type? For instance, in my data g(x)=0.10 occurs at w=2600 m for the hazard rate model and w=4300 m for the half-normal model. Is it correct to truncate each by these two different values, and then compare the AIC values between models? Or do I have to truncate by the same value for both model types if I'm hoping to compare AIC's? If the latter is the case, then how do I choose w if it differs for g(x)=0.10 between the two models? Thanks for any assistance!

messages.body_plain:
Brianna, yes, this is an issue - you cannot use AIC to select between models when truncation distance w differs.  It is unusual to have such a large difference between models.  Remember that g(x)=0.1 is just a guideline, and not the only guideline.  You want to choose a w to avoid having to fit the tail of the distribution, which can increase the number of parameters needed, and reduce precision and reliability.  Where 2 models differ by this much, I would tend to go for more truncation rather than less, suggesting something closer to 2600m than 4300m.  But I would try different values, and inspect histograms and goodness of fit stats, before selecting a single value to use across models.

Steve Buckland

Hi Rasmus and listfolk,

Thanks for your concise problem definition and taking the time to find
exactly where the error appeared!

The error you describe is raised to ensure that only observations that
were used to fit the detection function are used to fit the spatial
model -- so that the same data are used to fit both model stages. Since
the truncation distance is used to form the width of the segment,
including observations at greater than the truncation seems like the
wrong thing to do as the effort will not be correctly accounted for in
the DSM.

What is odd to me is that you would have binned data, so all of the
distances should lie within the bins. If you are able to send me (off
list) the data/code from running Distance in debug mode, I can
investigate further.

All the best,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
If you are adventuresome, know a little R and want to learn a little about reproducible research, you may want to try the package DsShiny which runs a shiny application in R to setup an rmarkdown document with your analysis from the mrds package. Shiny is an R package that can be used to create interactive web applications while accessing all of the power of R. RMarkdown is a document formatting system that uses knitr to encapsulate R code into the document making your analysis reproducible.

What do you need?  If you are using a recent version of RStudio then you will most likely have all of the packages you need but here is a list of the R packages you need to install:

1) mrds
2) shiny
3) rmarkdown
4) knitr
5) pander

You can get each of those from CRAN.  I believe RStudio also installs the  pandoc <http://johnmacfarlane.net/pandoc/> software which is needed.

Then you need to download the DsShiny package from DsShiny <https://drive.google.com/file/d/0B77g1ScdUwVeUzlEQkVCNm9kLTQ/view?usp=sharing>. Remember where you downloaded the zip file. Then use Install package from local zip in R or RStudio to install the package.

Once you get everything installed, in the R console enter

library(DsShiny)
create_document()

It will open a window in your web browser with several tabs.  The first is Features where you enter the features of your data. The second tab is where you enter the data files.  DsShiny assumes that your data are setup in 4 files following the conventions described in the mrds package.  The DsShiny package comes with the golf tee data files so you can see how the data should be formatted.  They are located in the DsShiny directory of your R Library on your computer (often stored under the R program directory).  The files are regions.txt (for region), samples.txt (for samples), tees.txt (for observations) and obs.txt (for observation-sample links). Once you load your observations they will appear on the screen.  You have the option then of binning your data.  The next tab is for the detection function and what appears there will depend on whether you chose single or double observer data.  Once you have made your selections, click on the fit model button and the tabs with histograms, gof etc will be populated.  You can then click on Abundance and finally on Record. Once you hit the record and stop button the browser screen will be greyed out and control will return to your R console where the rmarkdown document is returned and processed.  The result will appear in a browser window.  You can also use
create_document(type="word") and the results will appear in the word document.  If you have a Latex system on your computer (eg Mkitex also free) then you can also use type="pdf".  Regardless, the file distance_knitr.rmd in your current working directory is the file of interest because it is the reproducible research document that you should use.  It contains the R code used for mrds which will help you construct your own calls to mrds. You can modify the rmd document as you see fit and then reconstruct an html,word r pdf(if you have Latex) and use it as the starting point of your manuscript.  You also need the file data.csv which was constructed with your original data.

This is all easier if you are using Rstudio because you can then open the .rmd document in Rstudio, edit it and then re-knit it. This is just a first cut at DsShiny.  If you have suggestions or problems send them my way. There is more to do there.

regards --jeff

Hi Rasmus (hi list!),

If you wish to get this analysis working in Distance I think you'll have
to re-import the data, but you have a few options in how you do this.

I think I was able to duplicate your bug using the dolphin example in R:

library(dsm)
library(Distance)

data(mexdolphins)

hr.model <- ds(mexdolphins$distdata, 7000, key ="hn",
	       adjustment = NULL, cutpoints=c(0,2000,4500,6000,7000))

mod1<-dsm(N~s(x,y), hr.model, mexdolphins$segdata, mexdolphins$obsdata)

The check that is implemented is to check that the column "distance" in
the observation data is not greater than the truncation. So here are
some options:

1) Remove the "distance" column in the observation data and re-import
into Distance -- this removes the check, giving you what you had before.
As I said in the previous e-mail, this will mean that the per-segment
effort is incorrect. In R one can simply perform (using the above as an
example:

mexdolphins$obsdata$distance <- NULL

2) Remove observations with observed distance larger than the
truncation. This is relatively simple in R (using the above as an example):

mexdolphins$obsdata <-
mexdolphins$obsdata[mexdolphins$obsdata$distance<=7000,])

You can then use write.csv() to write out the data.frame and re-import
into Distance (or carry on your analysis in R).

I hope this helps!

best,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mary & list,

If I understand correctly, you want just the number "unique" animals
observed during a double observer survey, ignoring the duplicates but
taking into account group size?

Each observation has two rows in the data.frame, one for observer 1 and
one for observer 2 (and each has a detected entry of 0 or 1, depending
on whether the animal/cluster was missed or detected by each observer),
to occur in the data set the animal or cluster must be seen at least once.

So simply summing the size column and dividing by 2 should give the
correct answer. Before believing the result, you may want to verify that
each observation is in the data twice, we can check that by looking at
the number of times that each object ID appears in the data.

Using the golf tee data that's shipped with mrds as an example:

# load data & give it a short name
data(book.tee.data)
bt <- book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe

# check that each object is in the data twice:
all(table(bt$object)==2)

# if this is fine, calculate
sum(bt$size)/2
# alternatively verify with
sum(bt$size[bt$observer==1])
# and
sum(bt$size[bt$observer==2])

(Comparing the result from the last two lines above also checks that the
group size is reported identically for both observers.)

Hope this helps!

best,
--dave

in one zip here https://github.com/dill/soap_checker/archive/master.zip

If you wish to get this analysis working in Distance I think you'll have to re-import the data, but you have a few options in how you do this.

library(dsm)
library(Distance)

data(mexdolphins)

hr.model <- ds(mexdolphins$distdata, 7000, key ="hn",

mod1<-dsm(N~s(x,y), hr.model, mexdolphins$segdata, mexdolphins$obsdata)

The check that is implemented is to check that the column "distance" in the observation data is not greater than the truncation. So here are some options:

1) Remove the "distance" column in the observation data and re-import into Distance -- this removes the check, giving you what you had before.
As I said in the previous e-mail, this will mean that the per-segment effort is incorrect. In R one can simply perform (using the above as an
example:

mexdolphins$obsdata$distance <- NULL

mexdolphins$obsdata <-
mexdolphins$obsdata[mexdolphins$obsdata$distance<=7000,])

You can then use write.csv() to write out the data.frame and re-import into Distance (or carry on your analysis in R).

I hope this helps!

Hi Adrian,

Currently DSsim requires you to provide a list for the gaps even if there are none.. looks like something I could improve in the package however and I will take a look later in the week.

To make it work at the moment use this code in addition to what you have written:

gaps <- list()
gaps[[1]] <- list(data.frame(x=0, y = 0))
region <- make.region(region.name <http://region.name>="SantaCruz", units="m", coords = coords, gaps = gaps)

Then you can plot your region:

plot(region)

I would change the name of your region object from Region to region as Region is the class name.

As for your earlier question, you have to load the shapefile using the shapefile library and then pass in the shapefile object:

library(shapefiles)
region.shapefile <- read.shapefile("Region")
region <- make.region(region.name <http://region.name> = "Survey Region", units = "m", shapefile = region.shapefile)

"Region" is the name of your shapefile file with no extension so you will be loading  the following 3 files into the object region.shapefile all at once: Region.shp, Region.shx and Region.dbf

Let me know if you run into any further issues.

The density.surface argument to the make.density command should be a list of dataframes with one dataframe for each strata. The dataframes should have columns x, y and density as you have created. The following should work:

densidad.list <- list()
densidad.list[[1]] <- densidad.pred
make.density(region.obj=region, density.surface = densidad.list, 885.88, 885.88)

The detectability object is not optional it is required by the simulation. This determines the probability of detecting the animals based on their distance from the transect and allows the DSsim so simulate detections.

After you have defined the region, density, population and detectability you can create an instance of a population. However, it is easier to create the simulation object as a whole and then do what you want with it: generate.population, generate.transects, create.survey.results, run. The other oject you will need before you can create the simulation is the analysis list object, created using make.ddf.analysis.list(...).

Hello Distance Sampling Community:
We seem to have come across some confusing data with our research project.  We are performing double-observer distance sampling aerial surveys for large mammals.  We have completed three sets of surveys so far and have ran the data through Distance (MRDS engine).  We took the data and ran it as conventional distance sampling (CDS  engine) so that we could compare the two techniques. We had fully expected for the CDS data to be lower than the MRDS data. However, our CDS values are much higher than our MRDS values. The CDS values are accompanied by higher CV's and wider confidence intervals.  We suspect the problem may be some sort of availability bias.  However, we haven't found solid evidence to prove or disprove this yet.  Does anyone have any insight as to what our potential problem could be? Is there an answer to why our CDS values are higher when it is expected for them to be lower than the MRDS values?
Any help would be greatly appreciated!!
